attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: 'Isn't going to change' is firm, unhedged language, so this is a scored forecast. The stated reasons are kept. No deadline is given.

contract.note: Reading 'change' as a material, causally attributed change in employment or hiring is a fair, ordinary reading of the plain words. Without a deadline, the claim can only be settled early by contradiction, which is appropriate.

evidence.note: Stanford/ADP preprint (Aug 2026) finds no economy-wide displacement but a 19% gap for young workers. The authors call these descriptive findings, not causal estimates, so they do not meet the bar of broadly accepted causal attribution.
Yale Budget Lab, as reported in Feb 2026, finds economy-wide stability so far. With no deadline, continued stability cannot confirm the forecast.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The early-contradiction rule needs broadly accepted research showing a material change caused by generative AI. The only signal, the gap for young workers, is described as descriptive and contested, and economy-wide data show stability. Stability cannot confirm a forecast with no deadline, so the claim stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: The drafter kept the 'don't even seem' hedge. That marks a tentative appearance judgment, not a firm assertion. Narrowing the scope to the restaurant systems is defensible from the context.

contract.note: The contract itself calls this a tentative assessment, yet it scores it anyway. It also supplies its own definition of whole-role replacement and picks the quarter. Policy applies plain-reading scoring only to firm language, not hedged statements.

evidence.note: NYT report (via Indian Express): Wendy's says 86% of orders need no human help. That measures how much of order-taking is automated, not whether jobs were replaced. No staffing data.
SoundHound vendor disclosure from March 2024, before the target quarter. It says the system aims to help employees, not cut jobs. This is a self-interested company statement.

reviews.rationale: 'Don't even seem capable' is a hedged, tentative judgment, so policy says it is not scored. Even read firmly, the packet has no staffing records that separate task automation from job replacement, so it could not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: Most clauses ('far too much', 'justify its existence') are value judgments. Only 'isn't getting cheaper' is factual, and it names no measure of cost.

contract.note: The same piece separates costs from prices: it says the technology is very expensive and that AI firms will have to raise prices. It also says the technology isn't getting much more efficient. So 'cheaper' points to the cost of providing generative AI, not API prices. Testing customer prices drops the speaker's evident meaning.

evidence.note: OpenAI cut GPT-3.5 Turbo input prices in June 2023. That is customer price, a different measure from provider cost. It is also a company statement.
GPT-4 Turbo was priced below GPT-4 in Nov 2023. Again customer price, not cost to provide. Company statement.
GPT-4o launched at half the price of GPT-4 Turbo in May 2024. Customer price, and it does not show provider unit costs falling.

reviews.rationale: The value-judgment clauses cannot be scored. The one factual clause, in context, is about the cost of providing generative AI, as Zitron sets costs against future price rises. The packet shows only falling API prices, which is a different measure and does not show provider costs. On the fair reading, the evidence leaves the claim unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his newsletter.

semantics.note: A present-tense, unhedged claim. 'Whole jobs' and 'early-career creative jobs' are reasonable glosses of his wording.

contract.note: Splitting the claim into task substitution, whole-role replacement and early-career effects is an ordinary reading. Using the quarter before publication is evaluator-selected but reasonable for a claim about the present.

evidence.note: Freelance-demand study with data ending July 2023, before the target period. It finds declines in writing and image postings but does not identify early-career workers or compare whole-role replacement.
Census survey running to Feb 2024, on AI broadly. Firms report substituting AI for tasks but few report job cuts. It predates the target period and does not cover creative early-career work.

reviews.rationale: Both items are consistent with parts of the claim, task substitution without whole-job cuts. But both fall before the target quarter, and neither measures early-career creative opportunities or generative AI specifically. No evidence in the packet settles the target period.
